abstract: This paper investigates how unsubstantiated elite claims of voter fraud affect public confidence in the electoral system. Using a nationwide survey experiment fielded after the 2018 US midterm elections, the authors examine whether exposure to fraud allegations erodes trust in elections. The study situates its findings within the broader context of efforts by political elites, most prominently Donald Trump after the 2020 election, to delegitimize election outcomes.
key_claims: Unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud by political elites have a corrosive effect on public trust in the election system.
The delegitimizing effect of fraud claims is a measurable, causal consequence of exposure to such rhetoric.
This dynamic is relevant to understanding elite attempts, such as Trump's 2020 efforts, to overturn or discredit election results through false fraud allegations.
methods: Nationwide survey experiment conducted in the United States following the 2018 midterm elections.
Experimental design exposing respondents to fraud claims to assess their effect on trust in elections (specific treatments and measures not detailed in the abstract).
findings: Exposure to unsubstantiated fraud claims reduces confidence in the election system.
The abstract indicates 'new evidence' of a corrosive effect, though full quantitative results are not available in the provided text.
contributions: Provides new experimental evidence on the causal impact of elite fraud claims on electoral trust.
Connects a 2018-era study to the broader phenomenon of election delegitimization, including the 2020 US presidential election aftermath.
framing: The paper is positioned within research on political elites, misinformation, and democratic legitimacy, focusing on how unsubstantiated fraud rhetoric undermines public confidence in electoral institutions.
